It's alright, I wrote a pile of text giving my detailed opinions on the game when steam graciously changed pages to warn me of an update and trashed my entire progress... I don't have the patience to write it again so here goes the short version with the important tidbits:

[list]
    [*] Orwell is a Visual Novel that tries to give a new coat of paint to the genre, kinda like Analogue a Hate Story. You read the plot through logs while doing your "job" of uncovering the truth. Props to the originality. Art style and UI is great and unique.
    [*] For a game that clearly takes upon George Orwell's work, it's not thought-provoking enough. It's very one-sided and not well written enough to make you really care. The only really Orwellian characteristic of this game is that the ending will thoroughly let you angry. It's not a bad thing given that the books 1984 and Animal Farm do just that, the real problem is that this alone can't give you a good experience when the ride there wasn't meaningful enough. The political thriller portion of Orwell is very stereotypical.
    [*] The detective portion of the game is great. If the game were focused solely on that with the political drama in the background, it could've been an amazing experience.
    [*] Decisions are very, [i]very[/i] poorly implemented. They don't change anything in the big picture and the branching path is the laziest type possible of a negative-sum game. You'll always see one side losing because the characters always act as stupidly as possible. To give a couple examples without spoiling anything, you have one witness that has an crucial information to prevent a disaster, and you can only get it out by blackmailing and ruining that person's life, keep in mind that by then you [i]know[/i] that person is innocent. The investigator assigned to help you is probably the most inexperienced and innefective cop ever seen when it can not even get a simple non-invasive information of someone who would cooperate if asked and not threatened. You'd argue that maybe this was the main critique of the game, but it was poorly implemented, it wasn't well written enough to make you believe such an absurd situation could ever happen. The same thing happens later when warning of an armed suspect prompts the investigator to give a "shoot ot kill" order when everything you have on the suspect is still circumstantial. Orders like "shoot to kill" are not so lightly given, especially not to law enforcement. Keep in mind that Orwell is NOT 1984, it's not the same envinronment and not the same setting, Orwell is closer to our reality than 1984's one.
    [*] For a game with so little branching paths, it's very short. 4 hours to finish it while playing leisurely
    [*] The dev clearly did not account for replayability. There's no option to skip dialogue or fasten the pace of the game. You can choose a chapter and that's all, choosing an earlier chapter will also void subsequent ones.
[/list]

That's basically it, you might think I have more bad things to say than good, that's something I adressed in my full review prior. Short version is: Given the price tag and the positive experiences throughout the game, I don't think it warrants to not reccommend because of that. I do want, however, that people know the game's shortcoming before buying. Most of these do not bother me and I'd probably still buy the game if I knew before playing, but some people wouldn't.

Orwell is more a graphic adventure game rather than the espionage game it was advertised as. If you like Life is Strange, you'd probably like Orwell. 
Sadly this is not my cup of tea. I want to actually think and *play* a game. If I want a story I'd watch a movie or a let's play... The story had to be deeper than this for me to be interested.

The good:
Orwell did a good job at designing the user interface. It's beautiful, functional, and believable. The artstyle is unique and pleasing to the eye.
You'd find that despite the handholding, you will have to make choices that will have separate story outcomes. Some choices are more "right" than others, There're be hints in the game to help you make the right choice, so the choices are at least not just random.

The bad:
However, just like the other reviewers had pointed out, the articles and character profiles are too simplistic, it doesn't feel "real" enough. This design choice is understandable since adding fluff and pointless information just for the sake of making the sites "real" doesn't help with immersion either. What would help with immersion is the compelling content; which I find sadly lacking here... I find myself just skimming through for highlights. It's too much hand-holding for my taste. Really, they could have made it so much better by just making the relevant text unhighlighted so we have to actually spend effort reading and playing the game as "intended".

[i]Orwell's[/i] premise is that you, clicking away at your computer, have been employed by a dystopian fragment of the future of western Europe ([i]a la Airstrip One[/i]) to prevent tragedies and [i]illegal crimes[/i], and piece together disparate - but (at least in the eyes of The Party) incriminating - evidence. In this sense, the player engages the narrative as something of a moral agent preceding artificial intelligence; selectively incorporating evidence into a portfolio of 'truth.'

If nothing else, know that I felt compelled while playing to consolidate my thoughts -- it's worth a second look. 

[b]Really neat:[/b] artstyle ([i]everything through the eyes of machines[/i]), 
worldbuilding (there's enough 'fluffing' information that it goes beyond the typical restrictiveness of VNs), 
polish (it's really very sleek, when it wants to be anyway), 
thematic presentation (a lot of the dialogue is very cheesy, but I'm consuming it all quite gleefully).

[b]Suboptimal:[/b] logical consistency (you can see clashes between "datachunks" yet-undiscovered...), 
obtuse gameplay (you can't redact erroneously-entered information, or supplement it with additional factoids... except when you can: on day 3, after deliberately avoiding embracing the alibi of one of the suspects, I dragged an absolving statement into their record without much thought and suddenly undermined my previous carefulness. Annoying, and little else.), 
frequently undue brevity (a supposed debate society with little more than waffling, news articles consisting of two paragraphs...).
achievement structure (story-tied and playthrough-exclusive, mandating inefficient replaying if you desire that category of completion)
Really fun game, eagerly waiting for more content from these guys.

You know all those safety measures we usually take (or fail to take online) for fear our personal info may be compromised and exploited by the powers that be? Well, Orwell puts you in the shoes of one of those people who collect such data. An outsourced data processor hired by the government.
Most of the time you will be selecting data chunks and uploading them to the mainframe of a huge, centralised surveillance hub. This explains both the concept and the mechanics of the game. The game is not linear and the story branches depending on your choices.

The story is fairly engaging, but the questions and dilemmas that the game deals with are even more compelling. If you are interested in the matters of online privacy, online identity, laws on privacy, data collecting engines or even just dystopia in general, this is a game for you.

That said, the game has its shortcomings in that the story, when you find out all the bits, does not really always add up in the most logical of ways, particularly if you choose some of the more exotic routes of the story.

Still, the experience itself is fairly novel, so this one gets an unreserved recommendation.

The premise is interesting, the UI is fantastic, but...

The writing doesn't work. Not to me, at least.

So the idea is, you're an anonymous member of the public working with a new program that's half google, half snooping software. You're assigned a case - the first one is about a bomb placed in a plaza, and thanks to surveillance cameras you're assigned to look up everything about a suspect. So far so good, right? There's the relevant question of whether it's right to spy on someone in the name of public safety, there's a mystery to solve...

But it falls apart. Your supervisor is all "she has a police record, let's snoop on her" and okay, good enough reason to investigate...her faux-facebook page, her faux-portfolio, news websites, etcetera. Except that none of these websites feel like they were ever used by real people, her facebook timeline feels bizarre, like she's a fascimile of a human being, and when you get to eavesdrop on her text messages with her boyfriend, again it feels false?

Everything is off, and not in a good way. And your supervisor is so ready to pin the entire case on her because she's joined an activist group that organizes protests against the surveillance state.

It's too on the nose, with writing that doesn't sell to me that I'm snooping on real people, with a wonky "this is taking place in real time" - but it's not, really, you only get to eavesdrop on people's text conversations when you unlock them, not when they happen - and it all just feels clumsy.

In a game that's only got its writing going for it, having a fantastically slick UI isn't going to keep me playing it. Which is a bummer! The questions this game is asking are relevant, and it's so slick and pretty to look at I want to dig into it! ... But sadly it's just not compelling.

Bummer.

Orwell is a surveillance game (I suppose you could call it). However, there is also a machine/program in the game called Orwell that gameplay centers around. 

The program seems to have two functions. The first is a tracking function: if the player provides a website, a chat handle, a phone number, an e-mail address, or even a computer ID (I suppose this is analogous to an IP address), the program will then "track" it. If a phone call comes in on the number, you can listen in. If a blog has an update, Orwell lets you know, etc. Often, you'll get a chat handle, then in the chat you'll find a phone number or e-mail, which you can then track. From all this data you can create profiles of persons of interest, which is the second function of the program. Through data, you can learn who knows who, and how they know each other.

Law Enforcement uses the information collected to locate and arrest those individuals that you've deemed possible suspects in crimes. The game begins with a bomb exploding in a public square. I won't give any more of the story away, because it's quite an interesting ride.

On the surface, this gameplay sounds straightforward, but there are juicy complications. For instance, if someone denounces the government harshly in a fit of rage after paying taxes, do they represent a danger to the government? If Orwell (the program) didn't have a human operator, could it read between the lines? To further increase the stakes, any data uploaded to Orwell is permanent. So I couldn't designate this hypothetical taxpayer as a threat and then clarify later that he didn't "mean" what he said.

Also, if someone was aware of the program, could they provide false meeting places to divert law enforcment? Do your persons of interest know that you know they know about Orwell? 

It's a very well done and thought-provoking game, especially in the age of big data. Not only does it explore some of the limitations of using data collection for crime prevention, but it makes the player realize just how much information about themselves they've made public online.

For instance, Judith Duportail (a writer for the Guardian) requested the data that the dating site Tinder had collected on her. In September 2017, she published an article detailing the experience. Tinder sent her 800 pages of material.

The game really blew away my expectations, I went in expecting a visual novel type story based around surveillance but instead got a gripping investigative mystery with a unique game style that I hope to see more of in future.

Looking forward to this studios next release, you've gained a fan.

[h1]A must-play for any cyber-security enthusiast[/h1]

[i]Received this as a gift from a dear friend[/i]

[b]Note:[/b]

Playing this game involves a lot of reading and if that's not your thing, you're probably not gonna enjoy Orwell.
But if you like playing VN's, I believe you'll love it!

[b]Gameplay:[/b]

You're an investigator in a secret mass-surveillance program run by the government, called Orwell (named after [url=https://youtu.be/h9JIKngJnCU]George Orwell, author of the novel '1984'[/url]).
Your job is to read up the information in your [i]Reader[/i] and upload [i]chunks[/i] of it to the Orwell database.
Uploading certain information may open up more leads and you may get unrestricted access to the 'target' person's PC, mobile, medical records and what not.

At certain times, you may find conflicting bits of information.
At such times, it's best to avoid resolving the issue. Read other relevant details and when you come back, it'd be clear to you what the right information is.

During the entire course of the game, all you do is read - a person's social network feed, their blogs. Sometimes you tap their calls and messages. But, you never directly interact with the individuals.
Yet, you gain so much knowledge about them that you practically know the person. Without actually [i]knowing[/i] them.
And all that just in the timeframe of 5 days!
It's kinda amazing and disturbing at the same time.

Also, the most important thing. Once an information is uploaded to Orwell, it cannot be deleted.
And there could be consequences depending on what you upload.
So, you wanna be careful, to not wrongly accuse an innocent. Which, trust me, is not that easy.

[b]My thoughts:[/b]
[i](May contain SPOILERS. Or it may simply affect your experience of the game. So read at your own risk ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ )[/i]

I loved the game.
Government mass surveillance has been a topic of concern for quite some time now.
It was ingenious to make a game that puts the player on the opposite side of the coin where the player is the one carrying out the surveillance.

At first, while it's all new and sunny, you feel like an unrivaled God - passing righteous judgments, punishing the wrong-doers. That is what you're made to believe you are.
And you find all sorts of crazy, unstable people in the world that you feel they [i]need[/i] to be surveilled.
Then you find out that they had a disturbing past that made them into what they are.
Then you realize that passing righteous judgments is a lot more difficult than you had initially assumed. And that personal data is a sensitive thing and it can destroy lives. And that YOU might be destroying someone's life as a part of your [i]work[/i].
If you're lucky, you'll wake up in time and realize how faulty the system is. And how you've been probing into other's personal lives and just how despicable that really is.
Otherwise, you either lose your humanity forever and become a Dementor that feeds on other people's personal lives. Or you go insane. Or both.

Maybe this journey of realization is similar to the one Edward Snowden had. Only, his journey was real and his actions had real consequences.
I would strongly recommend anyone to watch [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt3774114/]Snowden[/url] and [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt4044364/]Citizenfour[/url] after playing the game if you haven't already.

ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. 
After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. 
Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.”
Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.
Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is one of the most compelling, contemporary games available on Steam. Without pandering to any particular side, Orwell allows the player to explore the pros, cons, and grey areas of state-sanctioned surveillance. I highly recommend if you're into complex stories and games with multiple endings. I also recommend this game if you have a busy life and can only play short segments at a time...and don't want to be caught dead with Candy Crush or Bubble Witch Saga at the top of your play-time list. 

The only downside is that the game involves a lot (and I mean a LOT) of text. You're going to be doing a lot of reading. However, it's largely digestible because text is separated into news articles, web pages, and timelines (much like Facebook).

Orwell is worth the buy, even if it's not on sale. 8/10 would recommend.

There are moments that require choice, but far too few.  It is also unclear what effects different facts will have on the story, and the twists seems to be so obscure that I miss the point until the game points it out later.  Maybe I'm just dumb but I got confused too much and there's no way to backtrack without re-starting the game.

Its also very easy on resources, no mega PC needed to run it.  The stylised graphics are nice and add to the game but it adds to the issue with lack of obviousness and confusion.

Its certainly worth a play-through, its an interesting concept and clever story about privacy and security that makes you think and, in some places, evokes a real emotional response.  Its just a shame it didn't adjust the pace and make the twists a little more obvious once revealed. Then it would've been great.

The story is short but entertaining and exciting, you get the feeling of really becoming an Orwell 'investigator', the feeling is authentic, the websites, pages, profiles, articles, and that sort of stuff seemed believable enough to get you going into the story. Sometimes the story feels a little bit linear and forced upon you, e.g. pages that you need to look into for information will sometimes be spoonfed to you. but I get it though, if it wasn't though, many people won't know what to do next and get stuck, and they will need to add a lot more useless filler pages/information to make it a more realistic and harder experience. As typical with these kinds of games, there are multiple endings, all affected by your choices in the game. so it adds a bit of replay value.

I only hope they add more episodes/cases next, as the story is a bit short and there is potential for more storytelling using the Orwell system, I also hope they added in voice acting for the voice call tapping parts. so It feels even more authentic. 

I'd also not recommend it for it's full price at the moment(IF they add in more free episodes/cases, then I will change my stance about this, a Season Two is coming though, but that's for another price unfortunately). if you can get it for 50% off, I'd say it's now worth it. For me, I got it in a humble bundle monthly subscription that gives around $200 worth of good games for around $12 a month, along with Rise of the Tomb Raider and other more games.

Conflict:  Orwell is an excellent game that is well designed and well written. 

Conflict: Orwell is a poorly written game that is horribly designed. 

Choose one. 

Orwell is a game that would demand someone choose one of these options, and the problem is is Orwell is an very good game, that is well written.  It however has some horrible design choices that stop me from calling it excellent or perfect.  In fact these design choices are VERY problematic. 


The entire game of Orwell is viewing webpages/conversations/phone calls and hunting down information and uploading it to a major database.  You're allowed free access to almost anything and you can upload almost anything to the database and play with it.  You'll get chastised for uploading garbage information, but it's also kind of fun.  Then the government who hired you to find the information will eventually operate on what you have found.   The story is told through these uploads and the results of your information gathering will change the story.  That's kind of cool. 

And Orwell tells a compelling (if a little predictable) story.  However it ends abruptly and seems to think it's ending can be a lot more impactful than it ends up being.   And then it falls into an egregious hole of pushing replayability but not allowing players to replay part of the story. 

But the thing is Orwell doesn’t really explain it’s gameplay.  The core of the gameplay is not what you upload, but rather what you choose not to upload, or how you choose to resolve conflicts.   But I really hate how it handles conflicts.  What it should do is allow you to upload conflicting information and have you choose how to resolve it explaining more “what do you think?”  Instead it makes this assumption that A or B is right and whichever you choose, they kind of operate on.  However that’s not how the world works, there’s conflicts in a single paragraph and the question is does the guy feel remorseful or does the guy feel responsible for the past… the answer is probably both, why make me choose. 

Then there’s other conflics that seem to not matter.  But what’s really important is what doesn’t get uploaded, and that’s kind of the problem. 

The first game you’re going to upload everything, because that’s what you think is right, but the game is VERY interesting when you don’t upload everything, you can change the game and the story minorly because of this.  You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen. 

Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens.   I just want more interactivity in the story. 

The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent.  This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator.  I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail. 

You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same.  In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that. 

But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like.  There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story.  Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines.  And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time.  

However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it.  I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay.  I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive.

Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did.  I liked it that much.  10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale.  It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state.  But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story. 

I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy.  Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so.

Just off its writing quality, I would not recommend this game. 

I love many of the design features around this game, but honestly it just feels as though you are just scrolling down a page, looking for key words that are highlighted, and then dragging them into the information system. 

In games like this, the writing needs to be particularly strong if the game wants to retain your attention, and sadly, it is not particularly strong writing. I will refrain from completely degrading the work, as I appreciate the developer and writing team's attention to detail in the spirit of world building. 

Some moments which I really enjoyed were the conversations that you could overhear over a suspect's cell, though it is disappointing that there is no audio in these segments. The writers are successful in writing the story they wanted to write, but that does not mean that its perfect (but then again, nothing is).

Overall, I like this game, and I can see myself playing more of it, but I would not recommend it to many other people, as it is very niche. You really must be a person that is willing to read a lot of bland text in order to get a better feel for the world you're in. Ultimately, if you are interested in this game, you should be prepared to answer the question of whether your time reading in this game could not have been better spent in a good book, magazine, periodical, etc.

This game shows the tension between surveillance and freedom quite good. It's a better detective game without it being an actual detective game than most detective games...
Wrong conclusions because of too intensive or simply dumb surveillance is a big part of the game. These situations are easy to imagine to happening in real world surveillance, what is one of the biggest arguments against it. As there are a lot of such cases known in the real world, they wake you up and make you aware about the dangers of mass surveillance.

The gameplay is a bit lacking in this game. It pretends that you have a lot of freedom but this is only an illusion.
You play an agent which needs to collect information from all kinds of sources and put it into a system. This system then might or might not draw some conclusions from the found information. The conclusions are sometimes done by your supervisor who might trigger some action. These actions can be totally unintended by you and you might even think they endanger the investigation.

Sometimes there are pieces of information that you really don’t want to put into the system because wrong conclusions might be taken from them, but as the game seems to be linear (I haven’t been able to find a real alternative storyline yet, only small details that are different but not essential), you sometimes need to enter them to continue. The other way is true too, sometimes you got a piece of information in a source that cannot be selected to put into the system, while the piece of information is so basic you’re sure it’s missing and will be enabled later or entered from another source.

Although there are clear holes in the gameplay, the game is fun, and the freedom you get in the details let’s you still play a bit with how your targets need to live their lives.

Orwell takes sort of a visual novel framework and bends it until it looks something like a mass surveillance simulator. You're a foreign contractor working within a series of ethical safeguards to perform ethical mass surveillance (if such a thing is possible) for another country's government. And it's an interesting time to be an Orwell contractor, because The Nation is in the grips of a terrorist bombing spree. Your actions and possibly even inaction can bend the arc of the story.

Like most visual novels, your actions don't have major impacts on larger direction of the plot, but they change the details along the way and might make you more sympathetic to ending the game in one way or another. It's neat to go back and see how changes affect things and unlock other achievements, but it does get a little tedious since waiting through real-time chat and phone conversations is a lot less exciting the second time around.

Overall, I had a pretty good time, but most people will probably be one-and-done and put up fewer hours accordingly. Weigh that against how much you're willing to spend.

Orwell:

[h1]Positives:[/h1]

+ The story in this game is great. It covers a goverment project called Orwell, which collects information about citizens. You play as an investigator who is responsible for finding out who committed a series of terrorist attacks. By analysing social media, using phone wire taps and computer hacking, you will pry into the lives of suspects to find the true perpetrator. This is actually really fun and smart. The game does an excellent job of highlighting the problems with mass surveillance too and the plot twists will keep you guessing.

[h1]Negatives:[/h1]

- Because of the low budget, several areas of the game are not as good as they could have been. For example, when "listening" to phone calls via wire-tapping you aren't actually listening to anything - you're reading text which represents each character talking. There's no voice acting in this game at all. A real shame. Furthermore, the digital art sucks. The developers opted for really bizarre suspect photographs in newspapers or social media, which have lots of jagged lines on them. It's hard to explain, but the essence is the pictures in the game look really unrealistic and frankly, silly.

- Most of the game is reading and interacting with the investigator tools given to you. Occasionally you'll receives messages from your government adviser on data chunks you've assembled and their significance. There's literally nothing else in this game. At times it can be a little boring and you just wish there was more creativity, like video footage of potential suspects to review. Something a little different.

- The game is pretty short at about 10 hours. Some limited replayability though.

Overall Score: 7/10

This game will have you be FBI in a world where the NSA collects and store [i]everything[/i] but doesn't share it with you.

First off I rarely do reviews here on Steam but this game deserves it. Not because it's inherently bad game design, I don't think it is so much. Not because I just personally didn't like it or anything like that. I actually enjoyed the design choices both in terms of gameplay and aesthetics, it just works as is, nothing great but nothing terrible either. I have to review this and end up not recommending it because it's not even close to anything worth being called "Orwell". It's just not Orwellian enough, not thought-provocative enough. If you want to experience something more Orwellian just sign up on Facebook right now if you don't already have an account. It's even [i]"free"[/i]!

This game is overall a good piece of interactive narrative that can get you thinking about the implications of indiscriminately sharing every last little tidbit surrounding your life, and how that which you choose to share, along with other information available out there about yourself, can and will be used to create an image of you that might not necessarily be the whole picture. It's also good social commentary on the whole deal surrounding what makes an actual terrorist in today's world; This is immediately apparent as protesters early in the game protesting against mass surveillance because, well, mass surveillance, are portrayed as "anti-governmental terrorists" without much more context to legitimize that label.

What [b]this game isn't[/b] however is[b] a game about mass surveillance[/b]. As this is the whole selling point of this game I can't really recommend it, no matter how I otherwise enjoyed the game - for what it actually is. It's almost to the point where I would consider this to be false advertisement. You're not Big Brother, not even close. You're the In-Between Brother, looking down on Little Brother, bossing him around; But in the end both you and Little Brother are in a complete chokehold by Big Brother - no match, not even close.

What I'm trying to say is that this game does a good job of portraying how [b]directed surveillance[/b], what could be considered actual legit surveillance techniques, can be used to make decisions on who to pin crimes on after the fact. The game specifically portrays collection of information from social media as self-publicized, along with information gathered in general around the whole internet about a person, as this information is available when [b]specifically being looked for[/b]. That last part make a world of a difference. If a social media post has been removed by a user in this Orwellian future, well guess what, Big Brother can't see that post either. Orwellian, isn't it? Provocative, isn't it? 

The game does make some thought-provocative points around this theme of directed surveillance and social media content and in general hits the spot on that. In this day and age however it just isn't Orwellian enough, as what we have in our society today in terms of actual massive surveillance capabilities far surpasses anything remotely portrayed in this game.

So in conclusion, if you happen to feel that Big Brother-urge grow in you and all you want is to see how you would conduct yourself on the other side of the fence looking down on the sheeple, well look elsewhere. This won't be your fix. If you on the other hand feel like doing some detective work in a social media/online context and occasionally pin crimes on innocents for those authoritarian kicks, this might be your fix after all!

Got this game in Humble Monthy not really knowing all that much about what it was or anything like that, but jesus christ this was one of the most fun and unique gaming experiences I've had in a long time.

You're basically an investigator who has access to certain tools to sift through people's lives and search their phones/computers, monitor their conversations, and search for information on various websites about them. Your goal is to find out who committed a series of terrorist attacks and put them behind bars.

Now the gameplay here is obviously not the strong point. The only gameplay is really clicking and dragging blobs of test to the left every now and again. That being said though, it's not like you're mindlessly dragging things over and not doing/thinking about anything. You have to be cognizant of what you're uploading because you could screw up some stuff and let bad more things happen. Your choices matter, and there are multiple endings and possible situations that can happen in the game based on your choices.

The only thing I can say about the game is that I wish it offered more freedom or at least more thought to what you had to upload. There were instances in the game where it was just a linear click and drag whatever you see because there was nothing else to search. Then you get to episode 5 and you have to be careful of what you upload because you have a limited number of datachunks that you can actually upload before the story starts to unfold. I found that last episode much more interesting because of the fact that it forced you to actually read the documents and search through everything instead of basically just being able to drag the first thing you see. That and there were people by the end of the story that we didn't even get to investigate just because they were viewed as unimportant. Even with them not necessarily being related to the case, I would have liked to investigate those other people as well. This could actually bring more gameplay and they could easily relate some of those people to the suspects and have them tie in when them somehow.

Overall, if you like a game with an intriguing story to follow with serious attention to detail, then you will most likely enjoy this game. I usually don't like games with a deep story, but this game has such a deep and interesting plot that I have to recommend it. I'll definitely be picking up the 2nd one whenever it comes out.

I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass. 

The good - 
Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot. 
The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable. 

The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs.  There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer. 

Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice. 

At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue. 

I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game. 

The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) 
If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned.


There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. 

Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, 
"Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." 
and this narrative missed that promise.

An investigation game with an intriguing premises, [i]Orwell[/i] comes together as a unique experience that keeps you gripped with its narrative, despite fairly limited mechanics. Putting the player in the role of an investigator working with an information-processing system known as Orwell (referencing George Orwell's [i]1984[/i]), the game tasks you to search out information from a fictional set of websites (and later, live conversations and data on individual target personal devices) to investigate the aftermath of a bombing, to determine those responsible and various subsequent events.

The game's core concepts and the way in which the plot develops clearly link to recent contemporary developments, with surveillance becoming increasingly prevalent in many developed countries, and by the end of the game you're very much prompted to take the time to develop your thoughts on the merits of the 'real life' use of surveillance. In-game, this link to modern society serves to heighten the player's engagement with the game's mechanics and plot. Alongside this, there's a clean interface that minimises the friction in the information-gathering mechanics, well-judged use of music to emphasise key developments, and the ability to influence the outcome of certain poignant key events.

Man was I blown away by how great this game is, exceeding all expectations I had.
Great UI design, if at times lacking quality of life stuff(nothing major).
The story is great, the pacing is excellent, giving a real sense of urgency when it wants to.

The biggest gripe I have with this game is probably the lack of sound effects when listening to a call, making the calls feel like a slower paced version of the text messages. I'm not talking about voice over, just background noise and appropriate SFX would've greatly improved the experience, I feel.

All in all an amazing game that I recommend to anyone even slightly interested. :D

Orwell is a game with interesting concept, kinda like visual novel, the main mechanic of this game is gathering and filtering information via social media, article, document, etc.
The theme is about politics, freedom of speech, data spying, and spice of conspiracy plus drama (friendship, love, tragedy).

Overall, nice experience ^^

Orwell is a game about a powerful surveilllance tool that can gather information from the internet, chats, telephone calls and computers. You are an investigator whose job it is to gather said information of target persons.

There has been a terrorist bombing and we have a lead. So we start using the Orwell tool to gather information and spy on the targetted people thereby advancing the story. 

The whole gameplay is reading and clicking texts & images.

Depending on what information oyu gather, the story varies. But mostly you'll need to gather ~90% of all gatherable data to proceed.

Some Data is causes "conflicts". And here's the problem Orwell has: many of those "conflicts" don't make sense.
Example:
A: A person goes to the doctor, is examined and should stay at home to heal.
B: But the person doesn't agree and continues to go to work.

But: you can only gather information A [b]or[/b] B.
That makes no sense - as an investigator you should be able to gather A [b]and[/b] to get the whole picture.

If you want to hunt down achievemetns, there are several to gain which is great for replayabilty.
One playthrough takes 6+ hours.

All in all it's a good game  - I'd say 8/10
Good story, good length - got in a humble bundle I think.
